title: Jamie Dimon Warns Markets Are Underestimating Risks as JPMorgan Posts Record Quarter
excerpt: The JPMorgan CEO called asset prices 'elevated' and flagged geopolitical tensions, sticky inflation, and ballooning fiscal deficits as tectonic risks that could crack open at any moment.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • JPMorgan Chase reported record Q2 revenue of $57.35 billion and net income of $21.16 billion.
  • CEO Jamie Dimon warned of underlying risks like geopolitical tensions and sticky inflation affecting markets.
  • Bond yields have surged to levels not seen since 2007, impacting the equity risk premium.
  • Dimon cautioned that interest rates could rise significantly, indicating a potential bond market crack.

  • JPMorgan Chase posted record Q2 revenue of $57.35 billion and net income of $21.16 billion, beating estimates by the widest margin in five years
  • CEO Jamie Dimon warned that geopolitical tensions, sticky inflation, large fiscal deficits, and elevated asset prices are shifting below the surface like tectonic plates
  • Bond yields have surged to levels not seen since 2007, shrinking the equity risk premium to razor-thin territory
  • Dimon has repeatedly cautioned that interest rates could go much higher and that a bond market crack is inevitable

JPMorgan Chase delivered its strongest quarter on record last week, yet CEO Jamie Dimon used the moment to issue his starkest warning yet about the fragility hiding beneath booming markets.

Record Numbers, Cautious Words

The markets are booming right now, and it is pretty broad based, Dimon told reporters after JPMorgan posted second-quarter net income of $21.16 billion — earnings per share of $7.70 that demolished the $5.59 consensus. Total revenue surged 27.7% to $57.35 billion, with equity-markets revenue alone up 86% to $6 billion, according to MarketWatch.

Every business line posted record quarterly revenue. Investment-banking fees jumped 45% to $3.9 billion. Return on tangible common equity hit 29%, nearly double the 20.1% analysts had expected. The bank raised its full-year net interest income guidance to $105.5 billion.

"Several risks are shifting below the surface like tectonic plates, including geopolitical tensions and wars, sticky inflation, large global fiscal deficits and elevated asset prices."

— Jamie Dimon, JPMorgan Chase CEO

The Tectonic Risks

Dimon has been building this case all year. At the Reagan National Economic Forum in May, he called markets exuberant and pointed to Micron Technology’s sprint to a $1 trillion valuation — doubling in 48 trading days — as evidence of hype. Credit spreads are very low. So I look at all that as actually a risk, he said, according to CNBC.

In a subsequent Bloomberg interview, Dimon went further: They could be much higher than they are today, he said of interest rates, warning that the US government’s $30 trillion in debt, with an average rate of 3.5%, leaves almost no room for refinancing at lower costs.

His annual shareholder letter in April identified the Iran war and its inflationary ripple effects — particularly on oil prices — as the skunk at the party. If inflation creeps higher rather than lower, he wrote, this alone could cause interest rates to rise and asset prices to drop.

The Bond Market’s Warning

The numbers are already shifting. Thirty-year Treasury yields have climbed to levels last seen in 2007, according to Bloomberg data. The equity risk premium — the extra return investors demand for holding stocks over bonds — has compressed to what Rosenberg Research’s David Rosenberg calls razor-thin territory by historical standards, Barron’s reported.

Traders now price in a 70% chance of a Federal Reserve rate hike by December, a dramatic reversal from expectations of multiple rate cuts before the Iran war disrupted energy markets. New Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has signalled patience but not ruled out tightening.

What It Means for Investors

For diaspora investors with heavy US equity allocations — a common profile among Indian professionals in tech and finance — Dimon’s warnings carry particular weight. JPMorgan itself is preparing for both higher and lower rate scenarios, and the bank lowered its net charge-off outlook, suggesting consumer credit remains healthy for now.

But the juxtaposition is hard to ignore: the same quarter that produced $50 billion in trading revenue across the five largest Wall Street banks also surfaced conditions that Dimon says may remain manageable, but they could also cause meaningful disruptions when they shift or collide.

The five largest banks that reported last week are all trading at or near all-time highs. Whether that represents justified confidence or the kind of exuberance Dimon has been warning about is the question investors will need to answer for themselves.
